Every substantive wrong answer assumes that Dependent 1's generic "is disabled" flag satisfies SSI's aged/blind/disabled requirement. In the engine, is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled is False for all five members: Head is 48, Spouse 47, Dependent 1 27, Dependent 2 18 and Child 1 12. Because no member passes that test, SSI is $0 before any income, resource, deeming or living-arrangement test applies. The models' later steps (the full federal benefit rate, the one-third or PMV reduction, the Wisconsin supplement, the parental-deeming analysis) all compute a benefit for a person the engine does not count as SSI-disabled. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 0.0 to 11928.0 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. Under the alternative reading nine of the twelve models that paid SSI land within 10% of the $11,928 federal benefit (five exactly); deepseek-v4-pro, deepseek-v4-pro-0813 and inkling also applied a one-third in-kind reduction the facts do not support.

reference_bug_hypothesis: Wisconsin caps the net capital loss deduction at $500 a year (Wisconsin Schedule WD; DOR Publication 103). The engine instead treats Wisconsin's joint limit as $3,000 and adds back nothing. With the $2,500 add-back, Wisconsin AGI would be about $116,921, the sliding-scale deduction about $8,459, taxable income about $104,963 and tax about $4,758, not $4,599.62.
case_annotation: Wisconsin AGI equals federal AGI of $114,421. That is wages less the $2,315 traditional 401(k) deferral, plus $19,350 of partnership income and the $20,000 401(k) distribution, less the $16,800 farm loss, a $3,000 capital loss and the $108 IRA deduction. There is no SE-tax deduction because the farm loss more than wipes out the $14,000 of SE earnings, and the overtime premium is not excluded. The joint sliding-scale standard deduction phases down to $8,953 at that income, and five $700 exemptions come off income, leaving $101,968. That amount is taxed under the 2026 joint schedule, which includes the 4.4% bracket expanded by 2025 Act 15, and no nonrefundable credit applies. Models missed by mis-sizing the sliding deduction, dropping exemptions or treating them as tax credits, inventing itemized, school-property or married-couple credits, double-counting the SE partnership income, or using the older, narrower 4.4% bracket. Developer adjudication (2026-10-14): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (state_local_rule). The judge flagged the reference on the hypothesis that Wisconsin limits the net capital loss deduction to $500, and labeled claude-opus-5.5's row reference_model_issue_fixed because it applied that limit. The $500 limit is Wis. Stat. 71.05(10)(c)1., which covers only taxable years beginning before January 1, 2023; for 2026, subd. 2. allows $3,000 on a joint return, the $3,000 the reference deducts, so Wisconsin adds nothing back and the reference's Wisconsin AGI of $114,421 stands. The rows are model errors. Reference affirmed (Wis. Stat. 71.05(10)(c)2. (for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, a net capital loss offsets ordinary income up to $3,000, or $1,500 for married persons filing separately); 2025 Wisconsin Schedule WD, line 28).

Wisconsin's refundable individual income tax credits are the Homestead Credit, the Wisconsin EITC, the Farmland Preservation Credit, and the Veterans and Surviving Spouses Property Tax Credit; this household qualifies for none, so wi_refundable_credits and therefore state_refundable_credits are $0. The WI EITC is a flat percentage of the federal EITC (4%/11%/34% by number of qualifying children), and the federal EITC is $0 at $97,295 of wages plus partnership and 401(k) distribution income, so the WI EITC is $0. The Homestead Credit is barred both by its household-income ceiling near $24,680 and by the absence of any rent or property tax paid (only a mortgage balance is listed), and the Farmland Preservation Credit requires a farmland preservation agreement or certified zoning, which is unlisted and therefore false. The trap is arriving at an exact $0 rather than assuming that a household with a farm loss and Wisconsin residency picks up some small residual refundable credit.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The childless EITC has no minimum earned-income floor. It phases in at 7.65% from the first dollar of earnings, and a 40-year-old single filer falls inside the 25–64 age window. With $520 of wages and no investment income, the credit is 0.0765 × $520 = $39.78, and the other refundable credits are all zero. Nine models wrongly assumed the EITC needs a minimum or "substantial" earned income, or that it depends on tax liability, so they answered $0. One model got $39.78 and then replaced it with a made-up $234 from a table lookup.

Virginia expanded Medicaid, so a 40-year-old non-disabled citizen qualifies in the ACA adult expansion category if MAGI is at or below 138% FPL. Here MAGI is the actual $520 of wages, about 0.03x FPL. Eligibility does not depend on current enrollment: the 'other means-tested health coverage at interview' flag does not disqualify the head. The MAGI adult category has no asset test, so the $14,000 bank balance is irrelevant. The hourly rate and weekly hours do not replace the stated annual wages. Most models said No because they treated current coverage as a bar, applied an asset limit, or annualized $32/hour × 40 hours into income the head never earned.

This one-person Virginia household earns $520 a year, or $43.33 a month. That income is wiped out by the standard deduction, so net income is $0 and the benefit equals the full one-person maximum allotment of $298 a month, which totals $3,576 for the year. Models went wrong in two main ways. Eleven returned $0, mostly because they applied the regular SNAP asset limit to the $14,000 bank balance. They missed that Virginia's broad-based categorical eligibility, through a TANF-funded non-cash benefit, removes the asset test. Eighteen applied the right zero-net-income logic but used an outdated or guessed maximum allotment ($275–$300, most often $292 or $291) instead of $298. The rest made other errors: an invented income offset, an ABAWD time limit the household doesn't trigger because the head works 40 hours a week, or treating the annual wage as weekly. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (thresholds_rates). The frozen 3,596.04 is regenerated as 3,576.00: it applies the publication rule: SNAP October-December 2026 hold the FY2026 schedule (the SNAP uprating index behind the maximum allotments, deductions, shelter cap and utility allowances), the last USDA published before the 2026-07-03 reference freeze; USDA published FY2027 on 2026-08-21. The poverty guideline is the 2026 HHS guideline, published in January 2026. The engine's SNAP rounding defects are root causes r26, r27, r28 and r31, fixed upstream and applied with the convention. Reference regenerated (7 U.S.C. 2012(u), 2017(a); USDA FY2026 SNAP COLA memorandum (signed 2025-08-14)).

Virginia offers a refundable EITC equal to 20% of the federal EITC. It is paid even when Virginia tax liability is zero, and the prompt's take-up assumption means it is claimed. The head is a 40-year-old childless filer with $520 of wages, so the federal EITC is 7.65% × $520 = $39.78, and 20% of that is $7.96. Most models either said Virginia has no refundable credit, that the credit had expired, or that the federal EITC is zero. The rest found the credit but used the old 15% rate, which gives about $5.97–$6.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine sets dependent1's Medicaid MAGI income level from the dependent's own income, which is 0.00x FPL, instead of using the household of the parents who claim them on a joint return. Under 42 CFR 435.603(f)(2) and (d), that household's income includes the parents' roughly $87,302 MAGI, about 3x FPL for a household of 3, so the dependent would be above Indiana's 138% FPL expansion limit.
case_annotation: The answers split on whose income sets dependent1's Medicaid MAGI level. All 22 models counted the parents' joint-return MAGI of about $87,302 (wages plus pension) toward the 23-year-old tax dependent, which put them at about 3x FPL and ruled out expansion coverage. PolicyEngine puts dependent1's MAGI income level at 0.00x FPL because it does not count the $10,800 disability benefits or the parents' income. That places dependent1 in Indiana's ACA expansion adult category, which has a 138% FPL limit and no resource test. A few models made separate mistakes: some said $10,800 alone was over the single-adult limit, and some looked only at SSI-linked or asset-tested pathways. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_engine_defect; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (household_unit_or_filing_status). The frozen reference is 1.00; the alternative is 0.00. The prompt lists an adult 'Dependent' without saying whether that person is the claiming filers' child. If the dependent is their child, 42 CFR 435.603(f)(2) puts the dependent in the parents' Medicaid household, whose combined MAGI decides eligibility; the reference treats the dependent as a non-child whose household is their own (42 CFR 435.603(f)(2)(i), (f)(3)). Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (the relationship of an adult tax dependent to the filers who claim them).

For anyone under 65, Medicare's disability pathway requires at least 24 months of entitlement to Social Security disability benefits (SSDI), or end-stage renal disease or ALS. Disability status by itself does not qualify a person. PolicyEngine checks age ≥ 65, then months receiving Social Security disability against the 24-month minimum, then ESRD. Dependent 1 is 23. Their 'disability benefits' input is a generic disability-benefit income line, not Social Security disability. Their months of SSDI receipt are not listed, so they count as 0, and ESRD is not listed, so it is false. Every model treated 'is disabled + receives disability benefits' as enough for Medicare. In doing so, each one assumed unlisted SSDI receipt or a satisfied waiting period, which the prompt explicitly says not to infer.

The reference uses current law, under which OBBBA made the TCJA structure permanent. AGI is $87,302 (wages plus pension). The dependent's own $10,800 of disability benefits is not on the parents' return. The 2026 MFJ standard deduction of $32,200 is larger than itemizing, because no mortgage interest is listed and net medical is only about $16,621. That leaves taxable income of $55,102, taxed at 10% up to $24,800 and 12% above it, for $6,116.24. The household then gets a $500 nonrefundable Credit for Other Dependents for the permanently disabled 23-year-old qualifying child, giving $5,616.24. The models went wrong in three main ways: using stale standard deduction or bracket figures (2024/2025 values, or a TCJA-sunset regime with personal exemptions and a 15% bracket); deducting the listed auto loan interest, which no fact makes qualified vehicle loan interest; and either dropping the $500 ODC or adding the dependent's benefits to the parents' income.

The 23-year-old disabled household member does not generate a refundable Child Tax Credit because the CTC requires a qualifying child under age 17. With no CTC-qualifying child and no eligibility for the other refundable credit components, federal refundable credits equal $0.

Ordinary age-based Medicare eligibility begins at age 65, and the 60-year-old head is below that threshold. No qualifying disability-based Medicare pathway or other exception is supplied, so the head is not Medicare eligible.

The prompt describes local_income_tax as covering 'NYC income tax, Philadelphia wage tax, Kansas City earnings tax, and St. Louis earnings tax where applicable.' Almost every model read that list as complete. PolicyEngine's local_income_tax also includes Indiana county income tax. It applied a default county (Adams, 1.6%) to Indiana AGI of $84,302, which is $87,302 federal AGI minus $1,000 per person in exemptions, giving $1,348.83. The prompt supports two readings: the four cities are the only taxes counted, or they are examples and any local income tax 'where applicable' counts. On top of that, the prompt never names a county, so even a model that counts Indiana county tax has no stated rate to apply. Developer adjudication (2026-10-10): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned prompt_ambiguity; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (state_local_rule). The prompt places the household in Indiana but states no county. Every Indiana county levies its own local income tax (IC 6-3.6), at rates that differ by county. policyengine-us 2.15.17 left county income tax out of local_income_tax, so the frozen reference was $0.00. From policyengine-us 2.23.1 (PolicyEngine/policyengine-us#9694, which standardized local income tax) the engine counts Indiana county income tax in local_income_tax, at the rate of the county it assigns a household with no stated county. The reference therefore depends on the household's county, which the prompt does not state. Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (county of residence (Indiana county income tax)).

The head is the only person with wages. Their $82,360 is taxed at 6.2% for Social Security ($5,106.32) and 1.45% for Medicare ($1,194.22), for $6,300.54 total. Those wages are below the 2026 Social Security wage base and the $250,000 Additional Medicare Tax threshold, and Indiana has no employee state payroll tax. The spouse has no listed wages, so the spouse's wages are $0, and neither the pension nor the disability benefits are FICA wages. The models went wrong by adding wages for the spouse, putting non-wage income into the tax base, or making rounding and arithmetic errors in the simple 7.65% calculation.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

reference_bug_hypothesis: The question explicitly lists Dependent 1 as "is disabled" with no earnings, which satisfies the disability criterion in 42 U.S.C. 1382c(a)(3). The trace still says no member is "flagged as blind or disabled in the engine's inputs" and returns is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled=False. This points to the benchmark's disability flag never reaching the engine's SSI disability input (is_ssi_disabled), so SSI fell to $0 instead of ($994 − $880) × 12 = $1,368.
case_annotation: The deciding step is SSI's aged/blind/disabled test. The engine evaluates every member with is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled=False: the head is 60, the spouse is 58, and Dependent 1 is not SSI-disabled under the engine's inputs. So SSI is $0 no matter what the income is. Every model instead took the prompt's 'is disabled' flag as proof that Dependent 1 meets the SSI disability test, then ran the benefit formula against $900/month of disability income. Twelve models arrived at ($994 − $880) × 12 = $1,368. The rest also misstated the federal benefit rate or the general income exclusion. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_data_issue_fixed; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 0.0 to 1368.0 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. Under the alternative reading 14 of the 17 models on the 46-model board that paid SSI land within 10% of $1,368 (11 exactly; nine of twelve, six exactly, when the output was excluded on 2026-09-05); glm-5.2, grok-build-0.1 and minimax-m3 used wrong rates or annualised the monthly exclusion. Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (42 U.S.C. 1382c(a)(3)(A); 20 CFR 416.905).

Indiana starts from federal AGI of $87,302 (wages plus taxable pension; the dependent's disability benefits are not in the filers' AGI). It allows only three $1,000 personal exemptions, for the head, spouse and the 23-year-old dependent, totaling $3,000. Indiana has no standard deduction and no extra exemption for a disabled dependent. The $1,500 additional dependent-child exemption applies only to a child under 19 or a full-time student under 24, so this dependent does not get it. That leaves $84,302, taxed at the 2026 statutory flat rate of 2.95%, for $2,486.91. Most models used an outdated or future rate (3.05%, 3.0%, 2.9% or 2.75%), invented a $1,500 disabled-dependent or qualifying-child exemption, or added deductions Indiana does not allow.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The reference uses wages of $34,083.53 as AGI. The $73,000 of educational assistance is excluded entirely, and the ESI premiums are not subtracted from the listed gross wages. It then subtracts the 2026 OBBBA single standard deduction of $16,100, leaving taxable income of $17,983.53. Tax is 10% of the first $12,400 plus 12% of the remaining $5,583.53, which gives $1,910.02, with no nonrefundable credits. The wrong answers fall into three groups. Some models put part or all of the educational assistance into income. Some used TCJA-sunset rules or 2024/2025 standard deductions and brackets instead of the permanent 2026 amounts. Others subtracted the refundable EITC, or credits the filer doesn't have, from a tax line measured before refundable credits.

Maryland Medicaid eligibility for this 31-year-old requires qualification through a specific MAGI or non-MAGI category. The head's MAGI income is 2.14 times FPL, above the applicable adult MAGI limit, and the head qualifies through no non-MAGI pathway, so the eligibility output is 0.

PolicyEngine's payroll_tax here is simply the employee FICA pair on the head's $34,084 of employment income: 6.2% Social Security ($2,113.18) plus 1.45% Medicare ($494.21), with the small cent-level offset from the engine's float32 wage representation. The trap has three parts: the FICA wage base is gross wages with no reduction for the $8,389 employer-sponsored insurance premium (PolicyEngine applies payroll tax to employment_income, not to a section 125 net-of-premium wage), the $73,000 educational assistance is student financial assistance rather than employment compensation and never enters the FICA base, and Maryland imposes no mandatory employee payroll contribution in 2026 — the FAMLI employee contribution is not in effect and is not part of this output. Every wrong answer comes from adding one of those three phantom adjustments, or from arithmetic that contradicts the model's own stated components.

Maryland AGI is just the $34,083.53 of wages. Educational assistance is not added to income, and the employer insurance premiums are not subtracted from the listed gross wages. Maryland's 2025 law replaced the old standard deduction (15% of AGI, capped at about $2,350–$2,850) with a flat $3,350 for single filers. That leaves $27,533.53 taxable after the $3,200 exemption, taxed at $90 + 4.75% × $24,533.53 = $1,255.34. Most models used the old capped deduction. Others added $67,750–$73,000 of educational assistance to income, subtracted the $8,389 of premiums from wages, added county tax, or wrongly zeroed out the tax.

Maryland’s refundable EITC is tied to federal EITC eligibility, and a single 31-year-old filer with no qualifying children and $34,084 of wages is above the childless EITC phaseout ceiling. The federal EITC is therefore zero, producing no Maryland refundable EITC or other applicable refundable Maryland credit.

The correct path runs as follows. AGI is $36,270: wages minus the traditional 401(k), plus interest, minus the traditional IRA and student loan interest. Subtracting the 2026 single standard deduction of $16,100 (OBBBA, no personal exemption) leaves taxable income of about $20,170. Tax at 10% up to $12,400 and 12% above that is $2,172.36. The Saver's Credit then applies at the 10% rate, because AGI falls in the single 10% tier. It is 10% of $1,924, which counts traditional and Roth 401(k)/IRA contributions and is under the $2,000 cap, so $192.40, leaving $1,979.96. The models split into a few error groups:
- Several dropped the Saver's Credit entirely.
- Several used TCJA-sunset law (personal exemption, 15% bracket) or pre-OBBBA/2025 standard deductions and bracket edges.
- Some used the wrong credit rate (50%) or a wrong contribution base (traditional only).
- A few invented credits that wiped out the whole liability.

The refundable Child Tax Credit requires at least one qualifying child; this household contains only a single 57-year-old adult. With no qualifying child and income above the childless EITC phaseout range, every refundable federal credit component is zero.

Illinois’s ACA adult Medicaid pathway requires income no greater than 138% FPL, while the head’s MAGI income is 2.27 times FPL. The head also qualifies through no non-MAGI pathway, so the Medicaid category is NONE and eligibility is No.

Employee Social Security and Medicare taxes apply to the full $38,000 of wages because the prompt lists $300 of health insurance premiums but never identifies them as a pre-tax cafeteria-plan deduction from FICA wages. The correct computation is $38,000 × 6.2% = $2,356 plus $38,000 × 1.45% = $551, totaling $2,907; the Additional Medicare Tax and Illinois employee payroll taxes are zero.

The Illinois calculation is simple. Base income is federal AGI of about $36,270 (wages minus the traditional 401(k), plus interest, minus the traditional IRA and student loan interest deductions). Subtract one inflation-indexed 2026 personal exemption of $2,925 and apply the flat 4.95% rate. There are no nonrefundable credits for this renter. Most models got the base right but used an older exemption amount: $2,850 (2025), $2,775 (2024) or $2,425 (2023). Others made structural errors: inventing a standard deduction, treating the exemption as a credit, adding back above-the-line deductions, excluding the health premium from AGI, or claiming a renter's credit.

Illinois's Earned Income Credit is calculated as a percentage of the federal EITC, so expanding the eligible age range does not create a credit when the federal EITC amount is zero. At this childless filer's income, the federal EITC has fully phased out, making the Illinois refundable credit zero.

Age 76 does not itself establish Medicaid eligibility, and this person qualifies through none of the Medicaid pathways represented by the engine. Their MAGI income is 2.28 times FPL, they receive no SSI, and the engine assigns medicaid_category = NONE; Medicare eligibility, housing assistance, and the mere availability of aged or spend-down programs do not create Medicaid eligibility.

Payroll tax applies to listed wages and other covered earnings, not to work hours by themselves. The household has no listed wage or self-employment income, so the employee Social Security, Medicare, Additional Medicare, and mandatory state payroll tax bases are all zero, yielding payroll_tax of $0.

Here NY tax is already zero, because the $20,000 pension/annuity exclusion for filers 59½ and older and the $8,000 single standard deduction bring NY taxable income to zero. That leaves only New York's refundable credits. There is no NY EITC or Empire State child credit, since the head has no earned income and no children. The refundable real property tax credit (IT-214) is also out, because household gross income counts all Social Security, and $31,320 + $5,222 = $36,542 is well over the $18,000 cap. Total NY refundable credits are $0.

Standard age-based Medicare eligibility applies at age 65 or older and does not require an explicit enrollment or eligibility-status input. The 80-year-old head therefore qualifies based directly on the listed age, regardless of household income.

Employee Medicare tax applies at 1.45% from the first dollar of covered wages; the high-income threshold applies only to the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax. On $20,000 of wages, employee Social Security tax is $1,240 and regular Medicare tax is $290, totaling $1,530 with no rounding adjustment.

The household's SNAP gross income is $73,974: $20,000 in wages, $34,608 in Social Security, $19,200 in veterans benefits and $166 in dividends and interest. Standard Medicare eligibility applies at age 65. The spouse is age 77 in 2026, so the age-based pathway yields Medicare eligibility without any separately listed enrollment or eligibility flag.

Both spouses fall in Michigan's Tier 2 birth cohort (head born 1946, spouse born 1949) and both are past age 67. That leaves Michigan income of about $20,166 (wages, interest and dividends), which the $40,000 deduction wipes out, so Michigan taxable income and tax are $0. Almost every model applied only the regular personal exemptions, and sometimes the special senior exemption, to that $20,166, so each ended up with a small positive tax.

Medicaid MAGI (42 CFR 435.603(e), which follows IRC 36B(d)(2)(B)) adds the untaxed portion of Social Security benefits back into income. That means the full $22,646 of SSDI counts, on top of the $3,108 pension. The head has no wages, so the traditional 401(k) and IRA contributions reduce nothing. MAGI is about $25,754, or 1.60 times FPL, which is above Michigan's 138% FPL limit for the adult expansion group. No other category applies: the head is 57, gets no SSI, is not pregnant, has no dependent children and has no disability flag, so the engine assigns medicaid_category NONE. Six models wrongly left untaxed SSDI out of MAGI or simply called the income 'low'. One subtracted 401(k) deferrals the head cannot make without wages. One treated SSDI receipt on its own as a disability route into Medicaid.

The head is 57, so the only route to Medicare is the disability pathway. That pathway needs 24 months of SSDI entitlement (or ESRD/ALS). PolicyEngine gates it on a separate count of months receiving SSDI, and the prompt says unlisted numeric inputs are 0 and unlisted statuses are false. With months of SSDI receipt at 0 and no disability or ESRD flag set, is_medicare_eligible is False. Every model treated the SSDI dollar amount alone as proof of Medicare eligibility, assuming or ignoring the 24-month waiting period instead of using the default of 0 months. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 0.0 to 1.0 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. In law the under-65 route needs 24 months of SSDI entitlement; a year-round recipient has at least 12. The facts do not settle it.

Employee payroll taxes apply to wages and other covered earnings, not Social Security disability benefits or taxable private pension income. With no wage, salary, or self-employment income listed, the employee Social Security, Medicare, Additional Medicare, and mandatory state payroll-tax components are all zero.

Most models applied the 100% FPL net income test or set the benefit to $0 once the contribution exceeded the maximum. Three models used the FY2025 $23 minimum, one used $25, and two inflated the medical deduction or the maximum allotment.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Employee payroll tax applies to wages and other covered employment earnings, not to Social Security disability benefits, pension income, IRA distributions, or tax refunds. The household has no listed wages, and the prompt requires unlisted numeric inputs to be zero, so the employee payroll-tax base is zero and the resulting payroll tax is $0.

The 2026 tax falls under the OBBBA, which made the TCJA structure permanent. That means a $16,100 single standard deduction, no personal exemption, and single brackets of 10% up to $12,400, 12% up to $50,400 and 22% up to $105,700. Ordinary taxable income of $86,960 is therefore taxed at $13,843, and the $6,226 of long-term gains and qualified dividends stacked on top is taxed at 15% ($934), for a total of $14,777. Nothing else applies: a 62-year-old gets no age-65 additional deduction or senior deduction, disability does not raise the standard deduction, and the Credit for the Elderly or Disabled is fully phased out at $109,286 AGI. The largest group of models assumed the TCJA sunset (personal exemption plus 10/15/25% brackets). Another group used 2025 or undersized 2026 standard deductions and bracket thresholds. A few computed $14,777 correctly but then submitted a different number.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Disability alone does not establish Florida Medicaid eligibility. The head qualifies through none of Florida's Medicaid pathways, so the engine assigns medicaid_category NONE; the 6.85× FPL income level also rules out any applicable MAGI category.

Medicare covers people aged 65 or older. Under 42 USC 426(b), people under 65 qualify through disability only after 24 months of entitlement to Social Security disability benefits, and there are separate ESRD and ALS pathways. PolicyEngine follows this rule: the age test fails at 62, and the disability pathway requires 24 or more months of SSDI receipt. This head has no Social Security disability income, since unlisted numeric inputs are 0, and has no ESRD or ALS, so the head is not eligible. Every model treated the generic 'is disabled' flag alone as enough for Medicare and skipped the requirement to have received SSDI for 24 months.

Only the $12,656 in wages is subject to payroll tax. Pension income, dividends and capital gains are not FICA wages. Employee Social Security at 6.2% plus employee Medicare at 1.45% comes to about $968. Wages are far below the Additional Medicare Tax threshold, and Florida has no employee state payroll tax. No model was misled by the tax base. The errors are arithmetic slips, a final value that contradicts the model's own correct working, and missing or unparsed answers.

WIC serves children only through their fifth birthday and generally requires household income at or below 185% of the federal poverty guideline. The model also inverted the income comparison: $173,820 is far above 185% of the poverty guideline for a three-person household, not 184% of the guideline.

The reference uses post-OBBBA 2026 law for a head of household. AGI is $164,220 (wages counted at the gross $160,000, child support excluded). Taxable income is $139,270 after the $24,150 HoH standard deduction and an $800 QBI deduction on the rental income. Exact 2026 HoH brackets (10% to $17,700, 12% to $67,450, 22% to $105,700, then 24%) give $24,211.80, and subtracting the fully usable $4,400 CTC ($2,200 per child) and the $200 CDCC leaves $19,611.80. Models went wrong in several ways: assuming TCJA expired (personal exemptions, $1,000 or phased-out CTC), using 2025 or older brackets and deductions, leaving out the QBI deduction, taking $6,480 of ESI premiums off the gross wages, itemizing with mortgage interest they made up, treating most of the CTC as refundable, or using the wrong filing status.

The Additional Child Tax Credit is not an entitlement of $1,700 per child; it is only the portion of the $2,200-per-child CTC that survives after the credit offsets tax liability, and it is further capped at 15% of earned income over $2,500 and at $1,700 per child. This head-of-household filer has AGI of $164,220 (wages $160,000 + rents $4,000 + interest $220; child support is not taxable), below the $200,000 HoH phase-out threshold, so the full $4,400 CTC is available — but taxable income near $140,000 after the 2026 HoH standard deduction and the QBI deduction produces federal tax well above $25,000, so the entire CTC is absorbed nonrefundably and nothing spills into refundable_ctc. EITC is zero on this income, and there is no AOTC, recovery rebate, or refundable payroll tax credit here, so federal refundable credits are $0. Every wrong model computed the ACTC cap and then reported the cap itself as a payment, skipping the tax-liability offset that defines the refundable portion.

Employee Social Security and Medicare taxes are calculated on the full $160,000 of wages in the computation trace; the listed $6,480 employer-sponsored insurance premium is not subtracted from the payroll-tax base. This yields $9,920 of Social Security tax plus $2,320 of Medicare tax, for $12,240 total, with no Additional Medicare Tax or mandatory Idaho employee payroll tax.

Self-employment tax applies only to net earnings from a trade or business, and the prompt lists no self-employment income. The $4,000 of rental income remains rental income and does not create a self-employment tax base, so the computation yields $0.

Idaho taxable income is $164,220 AGI minus the $24,150 2026 head-of-household standard deduction, the $1,000 Idaho dependent-care subtraction and the $800 QBI deduction on rental income, which gives $138,270. Idaho taxes head-of-household filers on the joint bracket: 5.3% on income above a $9,622 zero-rate amount, which comes to $6,818.34. No nonrefundable credits are subtracted, and the $10 permanent building fund tax is added, for $6,828.34. Most models used a repealed rate (5.695% or 5.8%), taxed the full taxable income with no zero-rate amount or used the single-filer amount instead, skipped the childcare and QBI subtractions, subtracted a $410 child credit, or left out the $10 building fund tax. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (state_local_rule). Idaho's $205 child tax credit applies only to taxable years beginning in 2018 through 2025, so it does not reduce 2026 tax; the judge's missing-credit hypothesis fails. The reference applies the Idaho zero-rate threshold held at its published 2025 amount. Reference affirmed (Idaho Code 63-3029L (taxable years 2018 through 2025); Idaho Administrative Bulletin, July 1, 2026, Docket 35-0101-2601).

Idaho's grocery credit is a refundable credit with no income phase-out, paid per household member (the filer and each dependent). Idaho HB 231 (2025) set it at $155 per person for 2026, so 3 × $155 = $465. About half the models used the old $120 rate (giving $360) or the even older $100 rate (giving $300). The other half wrongly called the credit nonrefundable or income-limited and answered $0. A few confused it with Idaho's $205 nonrefundable child tax credit.

The answer comes from a few steps. Wages are $26,006.18 and the net capital loss of $7,968 is capped at $3,000, so AGI is $23,006.18. The 2026 single standard deduction under the OBBBA-extended rules is $16,100, which beats $1,037 of itemized deductions. That leaves $6,906.18 of taxable income, taxed entirely at 10%, for $690.62 with no nonrefundable credits. Most models got this wrong in one of four ways: they used a stale or guessed standard deduction ($15,000, $15,350–$15,750), assumed the TCJA sunset ($8,300 plus a $5,300 personal exemption), took the $8,389 ESI premiums out of wages, or worked out about $691 and then submitted a different number.

The only potentially applicable refundable credit is the childless EITC, and its phaseout uses the greater of earned income or adjusted gross income. The $26,006 of wages is earned income; employer-sponsored insurance premiums do not reduce that amount, and at this earnings level the childless EITC is fully phased out. With no qualifying child or student and no applicable rebate or payroll credit, every refundable component is zero.

Louisiana's expansion pathway requires MAGI at or below the applicable adult limit, but the engine computes the head's MAGI income level as 1.44 times FPL, so that pathway fails. The listed employer-sponsored insurance premium is not established as a pre-tax payroll deduction and cannot simply be subtracted from wages; after the applicable MAGI computation, the head qualifies through no Medicaid category.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Employee Social Security and Medicare taxes are computed from the applicable payroll-tax wage base, and the reference calculation applies the 6.2% and 1.45% employee rates to the full $26,006 of wages. The employer-sponsored insurance premium input does not reduce that wage base in this calculation, producing $1,612.38 of Social Security tax plus $377.09 of Medicare tax, or $1,989.47.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Louisiana’s broad-based categorical eligibility gross-income screen does not itself guarantee a SNAP allotment; the household must still produce an eligible benefit under the net-income and allotment calculations. SNAP countable income does not subtract capital losses, a mortgage balance is not a shelter expense, and a non-elderly, nondisabled household cannot deduct medical expenses. With no listed deductible shelter payment and countable wages of $26,006, this one-person household receives $0.

Louisiana's post-2025 reform taxes Louisiana AGI at a flat 3% after a single standard deduction. That deduction is indexed for inflation starting in 2026, so the 2026 amount is $12,835, not the base-year $12,500. Here AGI is $23,006.18: wages of $26,006 less the $3,000 capital-loss limit. Subtracting $12,835 leaves $10,171.18, and 3% of that is $305.14. Most models used the un-indexed $12,500 and got $315.18. The rest fell into other traps: pre-reform law (the $4,500 personal exemption, graduated 1.85%/3.5% brackets, or the deduction for federal income tax), subtracting employer health premiums from the listed wages, or claiming Louisiana has no income tax. Developer adjudication (2026-10-06): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated reference_later_law (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 305.14; the value under the published figure is 305.05. The reference rests on a 2026 Louisiana standard deduction of $12,835, which policyengine-us computed from published CPI-U under R.S. 47:294(B) but which no Louisiana publication stated before the 2026-07-03 freeze; Louisiana's first 2026 return amount, $12,838, came in Revenue Information Bulletin 26-019 on 2026-09-28. Excluded under decision d994, which keeps the published-amounts convention for every other reference (reference_audit/2026-10-05-louisiana). Reference depends on law published after the reference freeze; output excluded from scoring (Louisiana Department of Revenue, Revenue Information Bulletin 26-019, dated 2026-09-28: Louisiana's 2026 standard deduction is $12,838 for single and separate filers and $25,676 for the other statuses, the first 2026 return amount Louisiana published).

The models applied Louisiana’s former refundable earned income tax credit, equal to 5% of the federal EITC, to tax year 2026. Louisiana no longer provides that refundable credit in 2026, so the Louisiana refundable-credits computation returns zero regardless of an estimated federal EITC amount.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

AGI is $200,136.91: wages plus the taxable $1,632 state refund. Under OBBBA the 2026 SALT cap is $40,400, and the $505k MAGI phase-down does not apply at this income. The engine's SALT deduction counts the $26,460 in real estate taxes plus Maryland state and county income tax, and that total is above the cap, so SALT equals the full $40,400. Add $28,210 of mortgage interest and itemized deductions come to $68,610, leaving taxable income of $131,526.91. The 2026 OBBBA single brackets (10/12/22/24% with breakpoints at $12,400, $50,400 and $105,700) then give $24,164.46. Most models went wrong on SALT in one of four ways: they counted only the property tax, counted only part of the Maryland income tax, used the expired $10,000 cap, or assumed the TCJA had sunset (personal exemptions, pre-2018 brackets). Developer adjudication (2026-09-29): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 24,164.46; the alternative is 23,772.80. The prompt lists state and local tax refund income without saying whether the refunded tax reduced federal tax in the year it was deducted; policyengine-us 2.15.17 counts the whole refund as income (policyengine-us#9422, fixing issue #9122), while under 26 U.S.C. 111(a) none of it is income if the household took no tax benefit from the deduction. Found in the 2026-09-29 engine upgrade (reference_audit/2026-09-28, cluster salt_refund_gross_income_9122). Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (whether the prior-year deduction of the refunded state and local tax reduced federal tax (prior-year itemization, the income-versus-sales-tax election, SALT-cap headroom)).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The requested local_income_tax output is limited to the separately modeled local taxes listed in the prompt: NYC, Philadelphia, Kansas City, and St. Louis. Maryland county income tax is not included in this output, so a Maryland household outside those modeled jurisdictions has a value of zero.

Others added a Maryland FAMLI contribution, which is not collected in 2026, or invented a Maryland payroll tax. Several models worked out exactly $14,317.32 and then submitted a different number.

The reference counts $881/month of SSI as unearned income. Both members are blind or disabled, their $1,045 in assets is under the couple limit, and the 2026 couple rate of $1,491 minus ($630 SSDI − $20) leaves $881, so gross income is $1,511. Because an elderly/disabled member has medical costs above $35/month, Arizona's standard medical deduction of $145 applies in place of the $26 actual excess. Net income is then $1,511 − $209 − $145 = $1,157, 30% of that rounds up to $348, and $546 − $348 gives $198/month, or $2,376 a year. About half the models left out SSI and landed near $5,000. For the EITC and the refundable CTC, wages count as earned income only to the extent they are included in gross income. The head's $3,859 of traditional 401(k) elective deferrals are excluded from gross income, so earned income is $5,914.72 − $3,859 = $2,055.72. The two-child EITC phases in at 40%: 0.40 × $2,055.72 = $822.29. The refundable CTC is 15% of earned income above $2,500, and that is $0 because earned income is below $2,500. Most models used the full $5,915 in gross wages, which produced an EITC of $2,366 and a refundable CTC of $512. Others invented exclusions, used the wrong refundable-CTC threshold, ignored the 15% earned-income formula, or treated the EITC as limited by tax liability.

Free school meals are awarded through two independent pathways, and this Montana household clears both: it receives $8,625.89 of SNAP, which categorically confers free-meal status, and its countable income of $11,979.68 ($5,914.72 wages plus $6,064.96 TANF) is 44% of the federal poverty guideline for a three-person household, far under the 130% free-meal ceiling. The two children, ages 5 and 6, are both school-age, so the free tier pays a $7.15 daily per-child subsidy for the contiguous-US school year, $2,261.92 annually. The trap is that SNAP and TANF receipt are derived outputs of this same household, not listed input facts, so a model that only credits explicitly stated benefit receipt loses the categorical pathway — but even the wage-only figure of $5,915 sits at roughly 22% of the poverty guideline, so the income test alone still lands in the free tier. Both models returned 0 without running either test.

The head is a 46-year-old parent of two young children with MAGI of about $5,915, which is 0.07 × FPL for a household of three. MAGI-based Medicaid has no asset test, and having employer-sponsored insurance does not bar eligibility. The wrong models used an invented FPL dollar figure, applied an asset test, or treated ESI as disqualifying. None of them compared 7% of FPL against the parent income limit.

Medicare eligibility below age 65 does not follow from a current disability flag alone; it requires a qualifying Medicare pathway, such as entitlement after the applicable Social Security disability waiting period or eligibility based on end-stage renal disease. The 46-year-old head has no listed Medicare-qualifying entitlement or condition, so the disability input does not change the result from ineligible.

WIC eligibility is individual, not household-wide: an adult qualifies only as a pregnant, breastfeeding, or postpartum woman, while merely caring for a young child does not confer eligibility. Texas imposes no individual state income tax, so a Texas resident has $0 of state income tax before refundable credits regardless of the listed taxable-income deductions or credits. Taxes from other jurisdictions do not apply because the household resides in Texas.

Stat. 71.52(6); Schedule H line 9d), which is the reading under the alternative value; the reference leaves them out.
